publishedSummary: Cardiac output is set by what arrives at the heart and what opposes its ejection. Preload, afterload and contractility are three separate handles on one pump, and most cardiovascular reasoning is a matter of asking which of them a change has moved.

sections.narrative:
Three independent properties determine what a ventricle ejects: how full it is when it starts (preload), how hard it must push to open the outlet and keep pushing (afterload), and how forcefully the muscle itself contracts at any given filling (contractility).

Afterload is the load or pressure that ventricular muscle must overcome during contraction. Its effect is specific and worth stating precisely: afterload mainly affects end-systolic volume. Raising afterload does not change how full the ventricle was at the start of the beat; it changes how completely the ventricle can empty, so more blood is left behind at the end of systole and stroke volume falls. Recognising that afterload acts on the end of the beat rather than the beginning is what makes its effects predictable.

Contractility is separate again, and can be moved without touching either loading condition. Adenosine illustrates this: adenosine inhibits cAMP production and reduces cardiac contractility. Since cAMP drives calcium entry and release in the myocyte, lowering it weakens each contraction at any given preload — which is why contractility is properly defined as force at a fixed filling, and why it can only be assessed once loading is accounted for.

The three interact once the pump begins to fail, and the interaction is what produces the clinical picture. When a weakened heart cannot initially pump the returning venous volume, blood backs up, raising right-atrial pressure. The heart is a pump in a closed circuit, so blood it fails to move forward necessarily accumulates behind it. Rising filling pressure recruits some extra force by the Frank–Starling mechanism, but it is also transmitted backward into the venous system — which is the origin of the congestive features of heart failure, and the reason that congestion and low output are two faces of the same failure rather than separate problems.

Blood vessels are not rigid tubes, and they are not simply elastic either. Smooth muscle in a vessel wall that is held stretched will gradually relax, and one that is held slack will gradually tighten. This behaviour, stress relaxation and its reverse, buffers the circulation against changes in blood volume over minutes to hours.

After blood-volume expansion, stress relaxation limits increases in mean systemic filling pressure, venous return, cardiac output and arterial pressure. The added volume initially distends the veins and raises the pressure filling the heart, which raises venous return and therefore output and pressure. But the distended venous walls then relax progressively, enlarging the reservoir to accommodate the extra volume, so filling pressure drifts back down and each downstream consequence follows it.

The response to loss is the mirror image: after blood-volume loss, reverse stress relaxation limits falls in mean systemic filling pressure, venous return, cardiac output and arterial pressure. The veins slowly tighten around the reduced volume, restoring filling pressure toward normal.

The common principle is that the venous system adjusts its capacity to match its contents. This is a slower mechanism than the baroreflex and a faster one than renal handling of salt and water, and it fills exactly that gap in time. It also explains a clinical observation that would otherwise be puzzling — that the haemodynamic effect of an infusion, or of a moderate haemorrhage, is often greatest early and partly self-correcting afterwards.

Two relationships connect the pump to the pressure it generates. Mean arterial pressure is determined approximately by cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance, and cardiac output itself equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.

Taken together these say that arterial pressure has exactly three proximate determinants: heart rate, stroke volume and peripheral resistance. Every influence on blood pressure — neural, hormonal, pharmacological or pathological — must act through at least one of them, which is what makes the pair of equations a genuine framework rather than an item to memorise. Faced with any change in blood pressure, the productive question is which of the three moved, and whether the others changed to compensate.

That compensation is why the equations must be read as a system. Because the terms multiply, a fall in one can be offset by a rise in another, and arterial pressure can stay entirely normal while the circulation underneath it is markedly abnormal. A patient losing stroke volume may maintain pressure by tachycardia and vasoconstriction, so a normal blood pressure is not evidence of a normal cardiac output. Equally, an intervention that lowers resistance will lower pressure less than expected if it allows output to rise.
